items.title: CRISPR is now being used to control genes, not just edit them
items.summary: CRISPR-based treatments that work by turning genes on or off are being tested in trials, and could be even more powerful than conventional gene editing
items.t: CRISPR is now being used to control genes, not just edit them

items.title: Vagus nerve stimulation slows growth and spread of pancreatic cancer
items.summary: An electrical implant around the oesophagus that stimulates the vagus nerve improved outcomes in mice with pancreatic cancer by making their tumours more susceptible to immunotherapy
items.t: Vagus nerve stimulation slows growth and spread of pancreatic cancer

items.title: The narwhal’s legendary “unicorn horn” holds a remarkable engineering secret
items.summary: The narwhal’s iconic spiral tusk, once prized in Europe as the horn of a mythical unicorn, conceals an extraordinary feat of natural engineering. Using advanced X-ray technology, an international team of scientists discovered that the tusk contains two intertwined microscopic spirals that twist in opposite directions.
items.t: The narwhal’s legendary “unicorn horn” holds a remarkable engineering secret

items.title: Scientists turn one of the world’s hardest-to-recycle plastics into high-performance lubricating oil
items.summary: Virginia Tech scientists have discovered how to transform one of the world's hardest-to-recycle plastics into a valuable ingredient for high-performance engine oil. Their innovative process converts discarded PVC into a useful lubricant material in just three hours. The breakthrough could turn a major source of plastic pollution into a valuable industrial resource while making lubricant production more sustainable.
items.t: Scientists turn one of the world’s hardest-to-recycle plastics into high-performance lubricating oil

items.title: New Scientist Book Club: How urine changed the course of human history
items.summary:
A detail from Joseph Wright’s 1771 painting The Alchemist Discovering Phosphorus, showing Henning Brand in 1669 Science History Images/Alamy 

Imagine you could boil the development of science down to a single ingredient. A magical, mystical compound that transformed human history. Of course, science doesn’t work that way; even if breakthroughs shift the paradigm of our understanding, discovery doesn’t progress like a tech tree in a computer game, but as an interweaving tapestry of complementary and competing ideas and experimentation. Theories can bubble under the surface for centuries, overlooked because of politics or failure to realise their implications, while innovations can emerge from taking an idea in one industry and transplanting it to another. But, for a moment, try and picture what just one such ingredient could be. What would you pick?

For centuries, in medieval Europe, alchemists quested for the “Philosopher’s Stone” that would finally help them achieve their dreams of transmutation. It was a search doomed to failure from the very beginning. And yet, a far better idea was under their noses – or, rather, their underpants – the entire time. My pick? Urine has a strong case for being the most transformative substance in human history.

The development of civilisation was built on chemistry. It required the first chemical reaction we mastered – fire – to keep us warm, cook our food and smelt ores. But leatherwork played an equally key role. Urine is a source of urea, which bacteria can break down…
items.t: New Scientist Book Club: How urine changed the course of human history

items.title: Read an extract from The Age of Alchemy by Kit Chapman
items.summary:
The New Scientist Book Club is reading The Age of Alchemy in December 

“ A handful of lime and another of sulfur in fine powder. 

Place them in a vessel containing strong vinegar or the urine of a small child. 

Heat it from below, until the liquid appears like blood. 

Advertisement 

Decant this properly, and use. ”

Unknown, Leiden Papyrus X , c. 300 CE 

In 1827, amid the dark, silent balm of an Egyptian night, a graverobber pulled a treasure from the sands. At first, the raider was frustrated; scavenging the tombs near Thebes, he had hoped to uncover a priceless heirloom, or a nugget of gold that would sparkle with lustre in the starlight. Instead, he had found only a clutch of rolled scrolls, made of papyrus and sealed against the elements.

For a moment, he considered casting the documents aside and leaving them for the desert. Then greed got the better of him. Westerners loved all things Egyptian, he reasoned. Since the French had arrived with Napoleon, the new field of “Egyptology” had swept the continent, capturing the imagination of scholars and the wealthy. It was almost as popular as the new science of “chemistry”. Surely, if he took his find to the market, he’d find some gullible fool willing to buy it.

The buyer’s name was Jean d’Anastasy, and he was anything but a fool. Born in Greece as the son of a Damascus merchant who had won and lost his fortune in the Napoleonic Wars, d’Anastasy had used his family’s connections to set himself up as a grain merchant in Alexandria, before scheming his way into being named the local Consul General for Sweden and…
items.t: Read an extract from The Age of Alchemy by Kit Chapman

items.title: Particles not seen before have been observed in a quantum simulator
items.summary: Physicists long held that all particles fall under categories of bosons or fermions, but a new experiment offers evidence that a third and long-debated class is possible after all
items.t: Particles not seen before have been observed in a quantum simulator

items.title: Scientists identify two ages when children may be most vulnerable to screen time
items.summary: Scientists have identified two potentially critical periods when screen time may be especially detrimental to children's learning and memory: infancy and the start of formal schooling. Greater screen exposure during these developmental windows was linked to poorer academic performance and weaker working memory years later.
items.t: Scientists identify two ages when children may be most vulnerable to screen time

items.title: Scientists discover signs of a hidden extinction crisis deep beneath the ocean
items.summary: The deep sea has long been considered a safe haven for marine life, but new genetic research suggests a hidden biodiversity crisis may be unfolding far beneath the waves. Scientists analyzing more than a decade of genetic data from five species of deep-sea fish and shrimp in the Gulf discovered troubling signs of extinction risk in every species examined.
items.t: Scientists discover signs of a hidden extinction crisis deep beneath the ocean

items.title: These bizarre prehistoric mammals may have been misunderstood for 150 years
items.summary: Giant horned mammals that emerged shortly after the extinction of the dinosaurs may have had far fewer physical differences between males and females than scientists once believed. The discovery challenges a classic example of sexual dimorphism and raises questions about how historical biases have shaped our understanding of extinct animals.
items.t: These bizarre prehistoric mammals may have been misunderstood for 150 years

items.title: For decades, scientists may have misunderstood how brain cells work
items.summary: A major new study challenges a long-standing assumption about how the brain works, revealing that most neurons are versatile multitaskers rather than highly specialized workers. By analyzing recordings from 43 regions of the mouse brain, researchers discovered that although some neurons are dedicated to specific functions, most respond to a wide variety of information in remarkably distinct ways.
items.t: For decades, scientists may have misunderstood how brain cells work

items.title: Ultracold atoms could help unravel a major flaw in quantum theory
items.summary: Standard quantum theory struggles to predict how long a particle will take to get from one place to another, but an experiment with ultracold atoms could help rule out some interpretations
items.t: Ultracold atoms could help unravel a major flaw in quantum theory

items.title: The surprising reason women seem better at multitasking than men
items.summary: Men and women appear to be similarly capable of multitasking, but men are more than twice as likely to ignore conversation while juggling multiple activities. Researchers believe this unexpected difference may help explain why women are widely perceived as better multitaskers.
items.t: The surprising reason women seem better at multitasking than men

items.title: Deep beneath Australia, hidden caves could unlock the secrets of alien worlds
items.summary: Scientists have solved the mystery of strange trenches scattered across Australia’s vast Nullarbor Plain, revealing an extensive hidden world beneath the surface. These subtle landscape features are created as deeply buried cave systems slowly collapse upward over millions of years. The discovery could help researchers locate unexplored caves containing ancient environmental records and unusual life forms.
items.t: Deep beneath Australia, hidden caves could unlock the secrets of alien worlds

items.title: This 345-million-year-old fossil had scientists fooled for decades
items.summary: A famous 345-million-year-old fossil has turned out to be something entirely different from what scientists believed for decades. Advanced X-ray imaging revealed hidden gills and thousands of tiny teeth, exposing a primitive aquatic or amphibious creature rather than an early reptile. The discovery suggests that several adaptations associated with life on land actually evolved in animals still dependent on water.
items.t: This 345-million-year-old fossil had scientists fooled for decades

items.title: AI solved the hardest problem in maths – is there anything it can’t do?
items.summary:
Alzheimer’s disease, involving amyloid plaques in the brain, will be tough for AI to solve JUAN GAERTNER/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY 

The progress AI has made in mathematics this year is nothing short of extraordinary. In January, I was impressed to see relatively minor open problems tackled with the help of AI . Now, AI is being used to solve the hardest problems in maths . The obvious next question is, if AI can do this, is there anything it can’t do? That is the inference that the AI companies want us to make, but, in reality, the answer is much more nuanced.

Read more 
 Mathematicians are amazed by ‘holy grail’ proof of Riemann hypothesis

We see this messaging in claims that AI can “solve X”, where X is any field of human endeavour you care to name. Biology is a big one. “Cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, mental illness – these will be relics of the past in, I think, less than a decade,” said Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei while promoting the company’s recent initial public offering . “I think one day maybe we can cure all disease with the help of AI,” said Demis Hassabis, CEO of Google DeepMind, last year , adding that this could be “within the next decade or so”.

This phenomenon isn’t new: I call it “physicist brain”, after the propensity for physicists to wade into areas outside their expertise and declare simple solutions. More broadly, it is called Nobel disease , after the many Nobel prizewinners who have gone on to make, shall we say, less evidenced-backed claims. In general, there is a tendency to think that if an intelligent person is good at one thing, they are…
items.t: AI solved the hardest problem in maths – is there anything it can’t do?

items.title: The defence tech revolution is changing how we innovate
items.summary:
Cpl Aaron J Stone/UK Ministry of Defence 

Only five years ago, defence technology start-ups had little choice but to wait for government funding to build and test their inventions – often in complex, multi-year programmes. No longer, however: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has prompted such a fast, furious response that military innovation timescales have shrunk dramatically.

“Ukraine is becoming a real-world lab for military innovation, and it’s innovating at a pace greater than anything that we’ve seen previously,” says Ola Fashade, an air vice-marshal in the Royal Air Force and director of military digitalisation and the rapid AI delivery task force at the UK’s Ministry of Defence (MoD).

“Agility and tempo of adaptation is critical. In a contested battlespace, technology that works well on day one, by day eight has become a little muted – and by day twelve it’s probably no longer relevant. And if you don’t adapt over that period, what you have is a very expensive and ineffective bag of steel.”

Advertisement 

That raises the question of how significant this accelerated innovation could become. In September 2026, New Scientist CoLab, sponsored by BAE Systems, brought together leading thinkers and investors from industry, the military and academia to discuss the factors driving this innovation and the lessons that can be transferred to other industries.

Staying alive 

The investment for this step change is coming both from the technology incubators based within military prime contractors – like the Launchpad incubator at BAE Systems – and from a host of…
items.t: The defence tech revolution is changing how we innovate

items.title: Scientists discover mysterious lakes more than a mile beneath the Red Sea
items.summary: More than a mile beneath the surface of the Red Sea, scientists have discovered rare underwater lakes that could reveal secrets about Earth's ancient oceans and the possibility of alien life. Known as brine pools, these extremely salty, oxygen-free environments are surprisingly teeming with microbial life, challenging our understanding of where living organisms can survive.
items.t: Scientists discover mysterious lakes more than a mile beneath the Red Sea

items.title: Astronomers may have discovered a black hole born before the first stars
items.summary: A mysterious object named Phoebe, detected when it briefly magnified a distant star, could be a primordial black hole formed just after the Big Bang. With an estimated mass only three times that of the Moon, it may be a 13-billion-year-old cosmic relic that offers new clues to the mystery of dark matter.
items.t: Astronomers may have discovered a black hole born before the first stars

items.title: Seabird ‘spies’ could help spot ships that aren’t broadcasting their location
items.summary:
A northern gannet ( Morus bassanus ) tagged with biologging devices on its back and tail Steve Votier 

Audio from seabirds fitted with mini recording devices and GPS trackers has been used by researchers to show that marine life can record encounters with vessels that are otherwise difficult to track.

Many large vessels are now legally required to carry automatic identification systems broadcasting their identity and location at regular intervals. Although this has allowed interactions between animals and fisheries to be studied at scale, there are enormous gaps in coverage.

In fact, recent research suggests that three-quarters of industrial fishing vessels don’t use the technology, says Jonathan Rutter at the University of Oxford. This is partly because regulations on the types of vessels that are required to share data vary by country. Large satellite “blind spots” also contribute to the problem, he says, and so does subterfuge for the purpose of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing (IUU).

Advertisement 

Read more 
 Most large fishing boats go untracked as ‘dark vessels’

Rutter says that being caught as bycatch in fishing is one of the greatest risks to seabird populations, but if fishing vessels are tracked only “with conventional methods, such footprints of risk may be strikingly incomplete”.

The team analysed audio collected from devices attached to seven northern gannets ( Morus bassanus ) and found that one third of the audio detections couldn’t be matched with vessel tracking data – mostly off the UK coast.

items.t: Seabird ‘spies’ could help spot ships that aren’t broadcasting their location

items.title: AI’s stunning progress in maths shows how little we understand it
items.summary:
MARK SYKES/SPL/Alamy 

There is a story, possibly apocryphal, that when the mathematician G. H. Hardy was about to undertake a dangerous sea voyage, he sent a postcard to a colleague declaring “I have solved the Riemann hypothesis”. Hardy, a staunch atheist, joked that this would prevent his ship from sinking, as God would never let him claim the credit for such a major result without revealing the details of his proof.

Hardy would probably be both astonished and aghast that we now have what seems to be a proof of the Riemann hypothesis , a problem that has vexed mathematicians since the 19th century, but that no one yet understands it. The consensus among mathematicians is that the proof, produced with the aid of AI, will hold, but that it will take much more work to make it comprehensible to humans.

However you feel about AI, this is a watershed moment, and one that demonstrates just how little we still understand about the capabilities of the technology. As recently as last month, leading mathematician Terence Tao speculated that AI would eventually solve the Riemann hypothesis, but that it may not happen before 2050. Now, some mathematicians are considering whether their hardest and most infamous remaining problems could be settled within months. In a year that has left mathematicians reeling, this may be the knock-out blow.

For non-mathematicians, the fall of the Riemann hypothesis is harder to interpret. In the past year, AI has seen incredible advances in…
items.t: AI’s stunning progress in maths shows how little we understand it

items.title: A cosmically close supernova may spill the stellar explosion’s secrets
items.summary: In early November, astronomers caught a nearby supernova. They soon realized it was something special and started scrambling to study it.
items.t: A cosmically close supernova may spill the stellar explosion’s secrets

items.title: Australia’s legless geckos evolved like snakes did
items.summary: Pygopods — Australia’s limbless geckos — have taken an evolutionary path more like that of snakes than of other legless lizards.
items.t: Australia’s legless geckos evolved like snakes did

Source
items.t: Novel Experiments Expand the Hunt for ‘Ultralight’ Dark Matter

items.title: A space telescope hunting for dark matter just discovered something unexpected
items.summary: ESA’s Euclid space telescope has discovered its first previously unknown comet, despite being designed to study distant galaxies and the mysteries of the dark Universe. The icy object is approximately 1.3 billion kilometers from Earth and follows an unusual orbit that takes thousands of years to complete.
items.t: A space telescope hunting for dark matter just discovered something unexpected

items.title: Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists
items.summary: Positrons are the antimatter counterpart of an electron. Physicists trapped a positron and cooled it to temperatures near absolute zero. Positron is suspended in a wall-free trap, safely separated from ordinary matter. Team will conduct most precise comparison yet between matter and antimatter. Any difference between the electron and positron could expose cracks in the Standard Model of particle physics.
items.t: Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists

items.title: What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach
items.summary: A new theory suggests that the brain may chemically encode and retrieve memories rather than relying solely on electrical signals. Researchers propose that interactions between brain cells and their molecular surroundings could help explain the intimate connection between memory, emotion, and thought. Their findings challenge the assumption that increasingly powerful computers could eventually develop human-like consciousness.
items.t: What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach

items.title: Physicists just sent an unblockable message through a brick wall using gravity
items.summary: Scientists have successfully transmitted a message through a brick wall using nothing but gravity, an old elevator, and an incredibly sensitive detector. By moving a massive counterweight between two positions, researchers encoded the word "Gravity" into tiny changes in gravitational pull. Unlike Wi-Fi or radio signals, gravity passes through ordinary barriers without being blocked, offering a potentially revolutionary way to communicate.
items.t: Physicists just sent an unblockable message through a brick wall using gravity

items.title: Extinct, long-legged grasshoppers walked on water alongside dinosaurs
items.summary: Clues in 99-million-year-old amber show why scientists think these insects could sit atop water and paddle across it.
items.t: Extinct, long-legged grasshoppers walked on water alongside dinosaurs

items.title: New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice
items.summary: A revolutionary new nasal treatment has restored youthful learning and memory performance in aging mice while preventing severe cognitive decline in mice with Alzheimer’s-like disease. Developed using technology similar to COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, the nose drops stimulate production of a brain-protecting protein that strengthens neurons and supports memory. Remarkably, the treatment preserved brain function without removing Alzheimer’s-associated plaques, suggesting a completely different way to combat cognitive decline.
items.t: New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice

items.title: A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star
items.summary: MIT scientists have discovered that tiny black holes left over from the Big Bang could slowly devour stars from within, eventually triggering spectacular explosions visible across galaxies. Detecting these unusual cosmic events could reveal the existence of primordial black holes and help solve the mystery of dark matter.
items.t: A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star

items.title: This man sometimes sees his cat’s eyes on people’s faces
items.summary: After brain surgery, he began seeing eyes he’d recently seen on other’s faces. The rare condition is providing insight into how brains perceive faces.
items.t: This man sometimes sees his cat’s eyes on people’s faces

items.title: Eagles can prey on adult baboons. Did our ancestors face that threat?
items.summary: Baboon remains with talon injuries reveal eagles can hunt large primates, suggesting human ancestors developed tactics to guard against such attacks.
items.t: Eagles can prey on adult baboons. Did our ancestors face that threat?

items.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick
items.summary: A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck has revealed sophisticated waterproofing techniques involving pine tar and beeswax. Microscopic pollen grains trapped in the ancient coatings are now helping scientists reconstruct where the vessel may have traveled and undergone repairs more than two millennia ago.
items.t: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick

items.title: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered surprising evidence that Earth’s next ice age may have already begun, only to be stopped by global warming. By studying ancient plants preserved beneath the Barnes Ice Cap in the Canadian Arctic, researchers discovered that the remnants of a massive ice sheet began expanding again about 2,000 years ago, signaling the possible start of a new glacial period. But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead.
items.t: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it

items.title: Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history
items.summary: Earth’s journey from an oxygen-starved world to a planet capable of supporting complex life may have unfolded very differently than scientists once believed. A new analysis suggests that oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere in three major stages, with the oceans taking millions or even hundreds of millions of years to catch up.
items.t: Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history

items.title: Math’s holy grail, the Riemann hypothesis, appears solved with AI’s help
items.summary: The proof apparently settles a 167-year-old puzzle related to prime numbers, thanks to a human mathematician working with AI.
items.t: Math’s holy grail, the Riemann hypothesis, appears solved with AI’s help

items.title: The notion of ‘positive masculinity’ is dividing the male studies field
items.summary: Masculinity has long been seen as a problem to be solved. Researchers disagree on how to flip the script so as to help men improve well-being.
items.t: The notion of ‘positive masculinity’ is dividing the male studies field

items.summary:
Humans have debated the meaning of life for many millennia, but from evolution’s perspective, it is simple: Preserve the genome. Of course, mutation is allowed, as is the genetic mixing and matching of sexual reproduction, to create variety and evolutionary diversity. But we all exist because a viable lineage of DNA has persisted for 4 billion years. The genome’s policy is typically…

items.title: ‘Mitt & Ted’ recounts how a political odd couple changed U.S. health care
items.summary: The newest season of The Big Dig podcast tells of how Mitt Romney and Ted Kennedy briefly joined forces to reform healthcare laws.
